Senses.Explanation: Not two rejects a proposed pair without replacing it with a general theory. The records test speech and silence, ordinary and holy, delusion and awakening, birth and death, and other stated pairs. Occurrences.Kwic: 第二諸菩薩各說入不二法門，以言顯於無言。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X83/X83n1578.xml). Record Pointing at the Moon (指月錄), Dazhu Huihai section: Dazhu Huihai speaks throughout the answer to a Vimalakirti lecturer; he distinguishes the chapter in which the bodhisattvas explain entry into not-two by using speech to display the speechless. Contextual case figures: Manjusri, Vimalakirti.

ContextActors.GrammarEvidence: The complete case explicitly names Manjusri in this inherited public-interview case.
The complete case explicitly names Vimalakirti in this inherited public-interview case.

Senses.Explanation: The gate of not-two is the Vimalakirti case’s challenge to meet what is ‘not two’ without freezing either speech or silence into the answer. Dazhu Huihai says the assembly’s speakers use words to display the speechless, Manjusri uses the speechless to display it, and Vimalakirti’s silence gathers up the preceding words. Yuanwu Keqin likewise says the verbal positions are swept away all at once. Yet the records refuse to leave the phrase as a settled label: an unnamed monk asks Dongshan Shouchu how to enter and receives ‘eyebrows three feet long’; an official asks Heyi Chaozi what it is and receives another concrete answer; Baiyan Fu says manifesting it would take three lives and sixty aeons; and Zhongfeng Mingben calls Pang’s paired warnings a direct route into the gate. The inherited case supplies the name, while public interviews turn it back into question, answer, appraisal, and warning against merely identifying it with muteness.

Senses.Explanation: Xuefeng Yicun counters Shishuang Qingzhu's formulas of resting, stopping, cold ashes, dead wood, and an ancient-temple incense burner with ‘without resting or stopping,’ followed by confused consciousness, tumbling disorder, crowded crossroads, thorns, blades, and fire. Yulin Tongxiu quotes the contrast and dismisses both elders' formulations as children's ball play. Tianyin Yuanxiu later quotes the same contrast and likewise calls both elders' raising of it children's ball play. The Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings transmits the formula between these two later appraisals. All three witnesses therefore preserve Xuefeng's one authored counter-formula, not three independent utterances.

Senses.Explanation: Not obtained by seeking outside is a recurrent denial that the matter, precept-body, or responsive capacity must be acquired from elsewhere. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that merely repeating 'originally complete, requiring no outward search' can freeze inquiry before it has begun. Other speakers apply the formula affirmatively to the precept-body or to capacities said to be already complete. The warning is part of the entry's meaning: the phrase denies an external source but does not authorize verbal possession without investigation.

Senses.Explanation: The proverb pictures someone unable to damage the boat taking the blow out on its bailer. Chan speakers use that displaced blow as a verdict on Nanquan breaking the cooking pot, on comments about Yangshan's hoe encounter, and on an inherited hall saying. Mingzhao Deqian adds the proverb after Nanquan breaks the pot; Jingqing Daofu uses it when asked about Xuansha's threat to kick over Yangshan's hoe; Po'an Zuxian turns it against Baoning's hall saying. An explicitly unnamed questioner asks Chengtian Chuanzong what the formula looks like; Chuanzong answers by raising a surrender flag. Yunmen Wenyan states it to his assembly, and when another explicitly unnamed questioner asks what great function appearing is, Yunmen raises his staff and loudly announces the old buddha’s arrival. Mingjue Cong also gives the formula as an answer before continuing his address. These encounters make ‘rules’ the fixed tracks or established patterns that the displayed function does not retain; the entry does not convert the words into permission for arbitrary conduct. The same wording occurs earlier in Sengcan’s Trust-in-Mind Inscription after motion and stillness are both brought to an end. Zhongfeng Mingben later quotes that line as a lemma and comments on it, preserving a textual lineage distinct from the great-function interview formula. The referent remains one predicate—retaining no fixed pattern—even though it appears in a verse and in interviews. Different genres and readings do not by themselves create different things.

Senses.Explanation: In the wild-fox case, 'not obscuring cause and effect' is Baizhang's turning answer; later comments question the fox's release and refuse to isolate it from the rejected companion phrase. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly contrasts the two phrases, while an unnamed monk inside the same commentary objects that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect' the fox body has not yet been shed. Dahui Zonggao preserves the paired questions but answers only by telling the questioner to raise them this way to people. Wumen Huikai asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game' (不落不昧，兩采一賽). Chaozong Tongren rebukes both rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, yet continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his own stated frame. Later records continue asking whether the pair is the same or different. The records preserve competing uses and questions; this entry does not select a winner among them.

Senses.Explanation: ‘It is not that there is no body’ is Baochi Yu's line in a portrait verse on Longya Judun: ‘The sun rises across the mountains; the full moon faces the door. It is not that there is no body; he does not wish to reveal it completely.’ The records then turn the verse into a bodily test. While Longya is sitting behind a curtain, an unnamed monastic quotes the second half and asks him to reveal himself fully. Longya opens the curtain and asks, ‘Do you see?’ When the unnamed monastic says no, Longya answers, ‘You did not bring your eyes.’ Baochi later says that Longya had expressed only half. Yunmen Wenyan has an unnamed monastic raise the case and says, ‘I do not mind telling you.’ The line therefore does not deny a body. It contrasts having one with making it wholly available to another's demand, and the curtain scene tests what seeing such a disclosure would require.

Senses.Explanation: Not to be polluted is Nanyue Huairang's answer when Huineng asks whether realization still involves cultivation and verification. Senses.Explanation: The phrase is a blunt valuation: something is not worth even half of one small cash coin. Nanshi Wenxiu spreads his hands and applies it to the teaching he has seen. Gulin Qingmao reverses a comparison between Kasyapa's costly robe and a king's jewel by declaring the jewel worthless. Daxiao Xingchong weighs three proposed explanations and dismisses one with the phrase. Touzi Yiqing says that what can rival the eight dragon kings in wealth when used is not worth half a coin when unused. Zhongfeng Mingben says a bamboo whip that once helped across a broken bridge is now worthless, while Miaodao closes a verse on the returning pine-planter with the same dismissal. The expression supplies the valuation; the surrounding speaker supplies what is being valued.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use “not established in written words” as part of the direct-pointing formula associated with Bodhidharma, but their own objections show that it does not amount to a blanket rejection of texts or speech. Yuanwu Keqin gives the familiar sequence—Bodhidharma did not establish written words, directly pointed to the human mind, and disclosed one's nature—then cites the Sixth Patriarch's warning that even the two words “not establish” have already established something. Dahui Zonggao contrasts the extensive canon with single transmission not established in written language and asks why the formula points to one's own mind rather than transmitting verbal subtleties. Mi'an Xianjie and Tianyin Yuanxiu deploy the formula as a concise account of Bodhidharma's coming. Zhongfeng Mingben argues that Sengcan's written Trust in Mind and the no-written-words saying can travel together without contradiction. Juelang Daosheng likewise raises Bodhidharma's use of the Descent into Lanka scripture as a challenge and answers that words can point to the mind. Guting Shanmi deliberately calls “not established in written words” a world full of verbal vines and “self-contradiction,” preventing an anti-text slogan from passing as the whole usage.

Senses.Explanation: Not free names constraint: inability to move or respond readily, or an inward unease that does not let a person rest. Chan records trace it to deliberate contrivance and to carrying an asserted object “on the mind,” while a public case reverses the complaint by asking when one was ever not free. Miyun Yuanwu gives the clearest causal chain: deliberate contrivance leads to not being free, which prevents quick response and becomes obstruction. In a letter he also takes up a layman’s report of a subtle unease in the chest and analyzes four causes. Luohan Guichen turns the word into a public test. When Fayan locates a stone inside mind, Guichen asks how constrained a traveler becomes by carrying that stone on his mind. The record also preserves reversals and contrasts. Zhenjing Kewen answers “when were you ever not free?” after Huanglong Huinan challenges his claimed freedom, while Dahui describes circumstances in which neither the person’s own nor another person’s situation lacks freedom. The inward discomfort and restriction on response remain one state of constraint rather than different things. The corpus supplies no basis for turning the adjective into a named technical category or permanent human condition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 恁麼說話。太殺壓良為賤。不識好惡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. Exact utterer: Dahui Zonggao. Dahui Zonggao judges his own preceding formulation too demeaning and unable to distinguish good from bad.

Senses.Explanation: Not knowing good from bad is a verdict on failed discrimination: the records use it when someone mishandles an encounter, mistakes explanation for accomplishment, or performs showily without judgment. Muzhou Daoming applies it to Baizhang’s staff action, while Ciming Chuyuan uses it against an elaborate exposition and Xuedou Chongxian against a stock answer. Linji Yixuan directs it at supernatural performance, while Dahui Zonggao turns it against an overdrawn formulation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 常不輕菩薩來也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1444.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhanran Yuancheng (湛然圓澄禪師語錄): exact actor (湛然圓澄禪師) owns the headword-bearing wording.

Senses.Explanation: Never-Disparaging is the figure who tells each person that they will become a buddha and refuses contempt. Chan masters bend that inherited act into public testing: one asks why he was not struck, another identifies unexpected objects with him, and later speakers announce his arrival.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase faults someone for failing to distinguish black from white, and in these records it names failed discrimination in an encounter or in teaching. Xuansha Shibei joins it to 'not knowing auspicious from inauspicious' when rebuking students who only trade replies. Zhu'an Zhenyan applies it to hearers who hide in a formula about forms having no fixed character. A later record quotes Fenyang Shanzhao's stricter pairing, 'right and wrong not distinguished, black and white not divided,' as disqualification from judging for others.

Entries.SourceTerm: 不逢出世明師、枉服大乘法藥

Senses.PreferredTarget: without meeting a discerning teacher who has appeared in the world, one takes the Great Vehicle’s medicine in vain
AlternateTargets: if one does not meet a clear teacher in the world, the Great Vehicle medicine is swallowed for nothing
SearchAliases: if one does not meet a clear teacher in the world, the Great Vehicle medicine is swallowed for nothing
Senses.Note: The medicine is Baozhi’s comparison for the teaching in this quoted line; the entry does not turn it into a physical remedy.

Occurrences.Kwic: 饒爾學得三賢四果十地滿心。也秖是在凡聖內坐。不見道。諸行無常是生滅法。勢力盡箭還墜。招得來生不如意。爭似無為實相門。一超直入如來地。為爾不是與麼人須要向古人建化門廣學知解。志公云。不逢出世明師。枉服大乘法藥。爾如今一切時中行住坐臥。但學無心。久久須實得。為爾力量小不能頓超。但得三年五年或十年。須得箇入頭處自然會去。為爾不能如是。須要將心學禪學道。佛法有甚麼交涉。故云。如來所說皆為化人

Occurrences.VariantForm: 不逢出世明師。枉服大乘法藥

Senses.Explanation: Baozhi’s line, quoted by Huangbo Xiyun, says that Great Vehicle medicine is taken in vain without meeting a discerning teacher who has appeared in the world. Huangbo recites the line after contrasting accumulated learning with entry through an old master’s teaching gate; he then tells his hearers to learn no-mind in every activity rather than seek another teaching to possess.

Yongjia Collection of the Chan School (禪宗永嘉集): Yongjia's Collection of the Chan School (禪宗永嘉集), in the letter headed Master Yongjia's Reply to Master Lang and signed by Xuanjue, records Yongjia Xuanjue writing that one may roam through mountains and valleys, range through the outskirts, and let the bearing wander freely. Senses.Explanation: To roam at ease is to go or stay freely without being tied or obstructed by what one meets. Yongjue Yuanxian defines it as remaining unattached amid false scenes, like a bird crossing the sky or a dragon leaving the sea, and rejects bondage to sights, sounds, wealth, or power as counterfeit ease. Tianhuang Daowu tells Longtan Chongxin to roam according to his nature. A compiler describes Danxia Tianran's going and staying this way; Tianyin Yuanxiu applies it to his staff; Shiyu Mingfang rejects crazed delusion under the name. An unnamed monk asks Lumen Fadeng about a person roaming outside things, and Yongjia Xuanjue uses the ordinary motion frame of roaming through mountains and valleys.

Senses.Explanation: Master Xiaoyao is the title by which the records preserve an otherwise unnamed successor of Jiashan Shanhui at Gao'an. This is a person, not the action of roaming at ease and not Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao. The Jingde Record places Xiaoyao Heshang on the Chan seat: Luxi states that thought after thought climbs after conditions while mind after mind is forever still; Xiaoyao says someone said that the previous evening, answers ‘I don't know,’ strikes Luxi across the mouth with the fly-whisk, and then addresses the assembly. The Patriarchs' Hall Collection independently says that Xiaoyao succeeded Jiashan and was at Gao'an, while acknowledging that it had not seen his conduct record and could not determine his beginning or end.

Senses.Explanation: A dull-witted bird roosting in reeds images incapable dependence on a confined place. Tianyi Zai sets it beside a trapped fish in a puddle and a person waiting by a stump for a rabbit, then compares such confinement with the World-Honored One’s closed room, the layman’s silence, and Bodhidharma facing the wall. The appraisal concerns incapacity and dependence, not merely a physically slow bird.
